clips.title: Why Terragrunt? | Theory
clips.why: A short theory video on the problem Terragrunt solves: the same backend settings and variables copied into every folder.
look: Why a backend block cannot use variables, so plain Terraform makes you copy it into every folder.
How one shared configuration replaces those copies.
Where each folder can still change what it needs.
clips.after: That shared configuration is our root.hcl: one remote_state block, and every unit's state path is made from its folder.

clips.title: Advanced Terraform and IAC lesson 7: Terragrunt Units
clips.why: The exact word we use, unit, explained: one folder, one terragrunt.hcl, one state.
look: A unit represents a small part of the infrastructure, such as one VPC.
Each unit has its own state.
The root file is shared code, not a unit; that is why ours is called root.hcl.
clips.after: Our ai-agents account is a set of units like core-services/vpc and sandboxes, each with its own state file in S3.

clips.title: How To Use Terragrunt to Manage Terraform At Scale
clips.why: A walk through a real root configuration in Gruntwork's example repository: remote state, generated files and shared inputs.
look: Where the remote_state block lives and how the state key is built from the folder path.
How generate writes provider and backend files into each unit.
How account and region files are read from parent folders.
clips.after: Our root.hcl does the same: S3 state per unit with a lock, provider blocks that assume the account's role, and tags from account.hcl.

clips.title: How To Use Terragrunt to Manage Terraform At Scale
clips.why: One minute that shows the result in the state bucket: one state file per unit, at a path named after the folder.
look: The state files are arranged like the folders.
Changing one unit only touches its own state file.
clips.after: In rhinohealth-terraform-state the ai-agents units will appear under accounts/ai-agents/... in exactly this way.

practice.q: Finish the first block of a new unit, so it receives the shared state settings and inputs.
practice.hint: A function that walks up the folders until it finds a file with this name.
practice.why: find_in_parent_folders finds the nearest root.hcl above the unit, so the same line works however deep the unit sits.

practice.q: Which line in root.hcl makes sure that two units never write to the same state file?

options.why: This says where Terragrunt writes the backend settings in each unit, not what they contain.
path_relative_to_include() is the unit's own path below the root, so every unit gets a different state file.
This reads the account's facts, such as the tags. Two units in the same account read the same file.

practice.q: The sandboxes unit needs the VPC's subnets. Finish the input.
practice.hint: A dependency gives you what the other unit returns.
practice.why: dependency.<name>.outputs.<output> reads the other unit's output. Before that unit is applied, the value comes from mock_outputs.

practice.q: You run terragrunt run --all apply in us-east-1 with a vpc unit and a sandboxes unit that depends on it. Put what happens in order.
items: Terragrunt reads every terragrunt.hcl below the folder and builds the order from the dependency blocks
It lists the units, vpc before sandboxes, and asks one question: y/n
It applies the vpc unit, which writes its own state file
It reads the vpc unit's outputs and passes private_subnets to the sandboxes unit
It applies the sandboxes unit with the real subnets
practice.why: The dependency decides the order, and the real outputs only exist after the vpc apply. That is also why one y applies everything: the reason this is a lab command and not something you run on a real account.

practice.q: You change one input in the sandboxes unit and run terragrunt plan in that folder only. What does the plan cover?

options.text: Only the resources in the sandboxes unit's state and module.
options.why: A plan in one unit runs tofu in that unit only. It reads the vpc unit's outputs, but it does not plan the VPC.

options.text: Every unit in the account, because they share root.hcl.
options.why: Sharing settings does not share resources. To plan every unit you would use run --all.

options.text: The sandboxes unit and the vpc unit, because of the dependency.
options.why: The dependency only reads outputs and sets the order for run --all. It does not add the VPC to this plan.
